query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: If the chemistry and integrity of the native oxide film on pre-exposure Q235 steel are modified to form a denser, less defective passive layer, then corrosion-related degradation in chloride-rich, room and elevated temperature environments will be suppressed compared to the untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure (as-rolled) state with its native, unmodified oxide film.
generation.intervention: Deliberate modification of the surface oxide film through controlled pre-treatment (e.g., a mild anodic oxidation or chemical passivation step) to enhance oxide film density and reduce defect density.
generation.conditions: Immersion in chloride-rich aqueous solutions (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) tested at room temperature and an elevated temperature (e.g., 60–80 °C) under controlled electrochemical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The structural integrity and composition of the surface oxide film, particularly its density and defect levels that govern its barrier properties against aggressive ions.
generation.mechanism: A denser, defect-minimized oxide film acts as an effective passivation barrier, reducing ion permeation and electrochemical reactions at the metal/solution interface, thereby suppressing the initiation and propagation of corrosion. In contrast, the untreated native oxide, being less controlled and potentially more defective, allows for easier chloride attack and localized degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel samples with the enhanced oxide layer will exhibit a higher corrosion potential (Ecorr), lower corrosion current density (icorr), higher polarization resistance, and evidence of a more uniform and adherent passive film (as confirmed by XPS/SEM) relative to untreated reference samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated pre-exposure Q235 steel with its native, non-optimized oxide film.
generation.boundary: Results are expected under controlled laboratory conditions in chloride-rich solutions at room and moderately elevated temperatures. Extreme environmental conditions or significantly different corrosive media may fall outside these findings.
generation.uncertainty: The precise impact magnitude of oxide modification on corrosion resistance may vary due to inherent variability in the native oxide film and its response to the treatment. Temperature-dependent kinetics and solution composition intricacies introduce additional uncertainty in quantifying effect sizes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of Q235 steel samples in the pre-exposure state. Subject one set to a controlled oxide film enhancement treatment (e.g., mild anodic oxidation or chemical passivation) and leave the other set untreated as a reference. Immerse both sets in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 70 °C). Monitor electrochemical behavior using potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) over a fixed period. Complement electrochemical testing with surface characterization (XPS and SEM) to assess the composition and defect density of the oxide films.
measurements: Corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (icorr) from potentiodynamic curves
Polarization resistance and capacitance from EIS spectra
Surface oxide film composition and morphology via XPS and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., higher Ecorr, lower icorr, increased polarization resistance, and a more uniform/dense oxide film) compared to the untreated reference under both temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that the modified surface oxide chemistry suppresses corrosion-related degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

The polarization experiments show that CoCrFeNiTix HEAs have excellent comprehensive corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. The presence of a passivation film is hypothesized to be the cause of the high resistance to corrosion. XPS investigated the chemical composition of the passivation film on the surface of the CoCrFeNiTix HEAs after the polarization experiment was investigated by in order to confirm this hypothesis. Figure 9 shows the XPS spectra of the passivation film on the CoCrFeNiTix HEAs. The passivation film is mainly composed of seven elements, i.e., Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Ti, O, and C. The Ni 2p peaks correspond to Ni and NiO. The Co 2p peaks correspond to Co and CoO. The Fe 2p peaks correspond to Fe and Fe2O3. The Cr 2p peaks correspond to Cr2O3. The Ti 2p peaks correspond to TiO2. The relative atomic percentages of Cr and Ti, as compared to the other metallic elements, are much higher on the surface of the passivation film than in the bulk material (from EDS analysis). Therefore, the main components of CoCrFeNiTix passivation film are determined to be TiO2 and Cr2O3.

chosen.technique: potentiodynamic polarization, EIS, and XPS/SEM analysis
chosen.conditions: Q235 steel samples in pre-exposure state exposed to chloride solutions under controlled room and elevated temperature conditions
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the mechanistic hypothesis by isolating the effect of the surface oxide film on corrosion onset and suppression. By deliberately modifying the oxide state and comparing against an untreated reference under harsh corrosive conditions, the study can decisively falsify or support the role of surface chemistry in corrosion degradation, which is a gap in earlier work that did not isolate this variable.
